items.name: Creatine monohydrate
items.evidenceFor: strength and muscle gains in people who lift or train
items.evidenceSummary: One of the best-studied supplements. For people who lift, it adds several kilos to strength gains over weeks of training; without training, gains are small. Monohydrate at 3 to 5 g a day is the studied form.
items.humanQuestion: Do you lift or train hard most weeks?
items.fitsInstead: Plain unflavored monohydrate powder, often around $10 a month.
items.notesInternal: Dose floor settled at 3 g/day. The ISSN 2017 position stand gives 3 g/day for 28 days as the low-dose route and says smaller amounts (e.g. 3-5 g/day) saturate muscle over 3-4 weeks; it never gives a 2 g human dose (it notes a normal diet already supplies 1-2 g/day). V3's ruleText cut-off of 2 g was wrong; the factCheck 3 g was right. Loading (~0.3 g/kg/day for 5-7 days, then 3-5 g/day) is optional; ISSN notes larger athletes may take 5-10 g/day. Female evidence is thin (Wang 2024: only 2 female-only trials, gains not significant). Wang co-author Candow advises creatine makers and most ISSN/Antonio authors disclose industry ties; Wang itself had no external funding and the strength effect is consistent (I2 = 0%), so A stands. FORM_NOT_ABSORBED: ISSN and Antonio find no form better than monohydrate and ISSN does not mention HCl, so for HCl or buffered the verdict should say monohydrate is the studied form, not that the other form fails; ethyl ester has the weakest case. tier_otherwise C: without training, gains are small and inconsistent (Antonio 2021, mostly older-adult data). V3's claim about thinking during sleep loss was not checked and is left out of person-facing text. Effect on sleep or HRV is not visible to wearables.

safety.note: Creatine labels advise a clinician check while breastfeeding.
Creatine looks safe for healthy kidneys, but with kidney disease a clinician decides first.
Creatine labels advise a clinician check during pregnancy, and safety data there are limited.
Many creatine labels advise against use under 18, though sports nutrition groups accept it for supervised teen athletes.

items.name: Protein powder
items.evidenceFor: muscle and strength gains in people who lift
items.evidenceSummary: Protein powder is food in a scoop. For people who lift, extra protein adds a little more muscle and strength, mainly until daily protein reaches about 1.6 g per kg of body weight. Without training, trials show little change.
items.humanQuestion: Do you lift, and does food alone cover your protein?
items.fitsInstead: Greek yogurt, eggs, tofu or lentils can cover the same protein at meals.
items.notesInternal: Tier A holds for people who lift, but the effect is modest (Morton 2018: +0.3 kg lean mass, +2.5 kg 1RM) and plateaus near 1.6 g/kg/day of total protein (CI 1.03-2.20; authors suggest ~2.2 g/kg/day may be prudent). A lifter already eating that much from food gets little extra; the brief allows only one evidence_requires value, so intake is a second condition the engine could ask about. Supplement dose was not a moderator in Morton (4-106 g/day used, 5-44 g post-exercise), so DOSE_BELOW_MIN is left out; dose_min 20 g mirrors the ISSN per-serving guidance (20-40 g or ~0.25 g/kg), not a proven floor. tier_otherwise C: Nunes 2022 found no significant lean-mass gain without resistance exercise (6 trials, low certainty). Phillips (author of both meta-analyses) discloses dairy and beef industry honoraria; Nunes 2022 was ILSI Europe funded with industry co-authors. Lead: the 2025 Consumer Reports testing is cited through an NPR/OPB news report, not a peer-reviewed paper; flagged for reviewer. Kind kept as supplement although V3 treated it as plain food (V3 had no tier rule at all). Proposed a show-together group with collagen for combined protein grams.

safety.note: With kidney disease, total protein is often limited, so a clinician sets the amount.
In 2025 testing many protein powders, plant-based ones most, exceeded a strict lead benchmark, so third-party-tested products are worth choosing.

items.name: Omega-3 fish oil
items.evidenceFor: heart health in people who rarely eat oily fish
items.evidenceSummary: For people who rarely eat oily fish, fish oil may help heart health slightly. Large trials, mostly in older adults, disagree, and the clearest hint of benefit sits with low fish eaters. Trials used about 850 mg EPA plus DHA.
studiedForms: fish oil capsules with EPA + DHA
items.humanQuestion: How often do you eat salmon, sardines or other oily fish?
items.fitsInstead: One or two meals a week of salmon, sardines or mackerel.
items.notesInternal: V3 graded B and said most positive trials were in people who don't eat fish; that is overstated. Only VITAL's prespecified fish-intake subgroup hinted at benefit in low fish eaters, and the authors call it hypothesis-generating (exact subgroup HRs sit in the NEJM supplement, which I did not open; vitalstudy.org returned 403). Hu 2019 could not test fish intake. Pooled RCTs show about 8% fewer heart attacks and coronary deaths in mostly older, higher-risk adults; Cochrane 2020 rates CV events as little or no effect (high certainty) and coronary events as a slight drop (low certainty). Hence C for low fish eaters. tier_otherwise D means no trial shows added benefit for people already eating oily fish weekly (the VITAL subgroup saw none); the scale has no 'tested and found little' grade, so D is the closest fit. Dose: V3 used both 500 mg and 1 g; set 840 mg EPA+DHA (VITAL dose; most trials ~850 mg; Hu range 376-4,000 mg). Count EPA+DHA from the label, not total fish oil weight (a 1,000 mg capsule often holds ~300 mg). New safety row: AF risk rises with dose (Gencer 2021, steeper above 1 g/day). V3's mood claim was not graded. Wearable set to no; small resting-heart-rate effects reported elsewhere were not checked here. No studies in 22-35-year-olds; all evidence extrapolated from older adults.

safety.note: Fish oil labels advise a clinician check for anyone with a bleeding problem.
In heart trials, fish oil above 1 g a day came with a higher chance of atrial fibrillation.
Fish oil labels advise checking with a prescriber when taking blood thinners.

items.name: Vitamin D3
items.evidenceFor: bone density and healthy vitamin D levels in people who run low
items.evidenceSummary: When vitamin D runs low, a daily dose brings levels up and supports bone density. With normal levels, large trials found little change in bones, mood or colds. More than 4,000 IU a day adds risk.
items.humanQuestion: Has a clinician or blood test ever said you run low?
items.fitsInstead: A plain tablet near 600 IU, often a couple of dollars a month.
items.notesInternal: Outcome chosen: bone density and levels when low, the one area where benefit clearly depends on baseline (Macdonald 2018: bone density rose only when starting 25(OH)D was at or below 30 nmol/L; the IOM found evidence for bone health only). Most 22-35 buyers want immunity, mood or energy, and those grade lower: colds C at best (Martineau 2017 showed a strong effect below 25 nmol/L, but Jolliffe 2021 and 2025 found no modification by baseline status and the 2025 overall effect is no longer significant); mood null (VITAL-DEP). tier_otherwise D means trials in people with normal levels found no bone, fracture or mood benefit (VITAL); the scale has no 'tested and found little' grade. B rather than A because the deficiency evidence comes from subgroup analyses of a few trials plus the IOM consensus. V3 nudged a ~$30 blood test: the Endocrine Society 2024 guideline suggests against routine 25(OH)D testing in healthy adults and against doses above the DRI for ages 19-74, and the IOM notes many labs use cut-offs that overstate deficiency (20 ng/mL, 50 nmol/L, is adequate for nearly everyone). Drop the testing nudge; ask whether a clinician already said it runs low. V3 put harm above 10,000 IU: the upper limit is 4,000 IU/day; above 10,000 IU/day is where kidney and tissue damage is documented. If clinician-prescribed (e.g. weekly high-dose), treat as clinician-led and protect. dose_min 600 IU is the RDA; DOSE_BELOW_MIN left out because correcting a deficiency is a clinician call. AG1 Next Gen reportedly has no vitamin D, so D plus AG1 is not an overlap (see overlap proposals).

safety.note: Very high vitamin D intakes can damage kidneys, so with kidney disease a clinician sets the dose.
Vitamin D labels advise checking with a doctor when taking other medicines.
Vitamin D is often advised in pregnancy, so any change goes through a clinician.

items.name: Multivitamin
items.evidenceFor: long-term health in adults who eat reasonably well
items.evidenceSummary: Large trials, mostly in adults over 50, found a daily multivitamin changed little for long-term health; one set of trials in older adults saw slightly better memory. With a varied diet, the added benefit looks small.
items.humanQuestion: Is this covering a known gap, or more like insurance?
items.fitsInstead: A basic store-brand multivitamin, often a few dollars a month.
items.notesInternal: C because the trials disagree slightly: the USPSTF evidence review pooled a small drop in cancer incidence (OR 0.93, 4 RCTs, limitations noted) while COSMOS found no effect on cancer, CV events or mortality; USPSTF grade is I (insufficient). V3 said there was no effect on cancer, which is not quite right. The cognitive benefit is confirmed only in adults 60+ (COSMOS, about 2 years of cognitive aging slowed). No trials in 22-35-year-olds. V3 also said it does no harm: USPSTF recommends against beta-carotene, which raises lung cancer risk in people at high risk (e.g. smokers), and some multis contain it. The safety list has no smoking condition, so this needs a reviewer decision. Targeted needs (B12 for vegans, iron, folate before pregnancy) are separate items and often clinician-led. COSMOS funders include Pfizer per the record; whether pills were donated was not confirmed.

safety.note: Multis with vitamin K can affect blood thinners like warfarin, so a prescriber checks first.
Multivitamin labels advise a clinician check in pregnancy, when a prenatal formula is usually used.

items.name: Greens powder (AG1 and similar)
items.evidenceFor: general health, energy and digestion
items.evidenceSummary: No independent trials yet. Every study so far was run or paid for by a greens brand, showing small shifts in gut bacteria and blood nutrient levels. Products like AG1 hold a multivitamin-level mix plus plant extracts.
items.humanQuestion: Is the morning glass the part you would miss?
items.fitsInstead: A smoothie with frozen spinach and berries keeps the morning glass for less.
items.notesInternal: Tier N per the brief's rule (brand-funded only counts as none). V3 said D. Every human study found was funded by the brand and/or written by its employees: AG1 (La Monica 2024: funded in part by AG1, two AG1 employees; Gonzalez 2026: AG1-funded, AG1 employees; Sapp 2026: five AG1-affiliated authors, no funding statement in the record) and Field of Greens (Robinson 2026: BrickHouse Nutrition paid for the trial and supplied the product). Kirby 2024 is a lab gut-simulator study by AG1 employees. Outcomes were surrogates (bacterial taxa, intake on paper, blood levels after one dose); none showed changes in health, energy or digestion, and microbiome diversity did not change. AG1 conference abstracts in JISSN 2025 supplements are also AG1-authored and were not opened. Price: AG1 is $79/month on subscription or $99 one-time per a Fortune review (Jan 2026, updated Jul 2026, affiliate-linked; https://www.fortune.com/article/ag1-review), so V3's $90 is updated to 79. The same review says AG1 Next Gen has no vitamin D or K (sold separately); the label could not be checked (drinkag1.com rate-limited). ritual_role is anchor because the morning glass often carries the habit, so fits_instead keeps the glass.

safety.note: Greens powder makers advise a doctor check while breastfeeding.
Greens powder makers advise a doctor check when taking medication, given the herbal extracts.
Greens powder makers advise a doctor check in pregnancy, as many blends include herbal extracts.
The AG1 maker advises a doctor check for anyone under 18.

items.name: Collagen peptides
items.evidenceFor: firmer, more hydrated skin
items.evidenceSummary: Trials paid for by collagen makers found small gains in skin hydration and elasticity after two to three months. Independent and higher-quality trials found no clear difference, so the skin case is unsettled.
items.humanQuestion: Is this mainly for skin, joints or hair?
items.fitsInstead: Daily sunscreen, which slowed skin aging over four years in one trial.
items.notesInternal: V3 graded B; the independent evidence does not back that. Myung 2025 (23 RCTs) found the pooled effect positive, but trials without company funding and high-quality trials showed no effect on hydration, elasticity or wrinkles. Graded C (studies disagree, split by funding). A stricter reading could give N, since the positive results come only from company-funded trials; reviewer call. Myung is abstract-only (full text paywalled), so subgroup sizes are unknown. De Miranda 2021 (19 RCTs, positive) did not assess funding in its abstract. V3's dose floors (5 g and 10 g) are unsupported: a positive RCT used 2.5 g/day (Proksch 2014; funding not stated in the record). The upper end of dose_typical (10 g) comes from typical products and V3, not from a trial opened in this session. Joint and hair outcomes were not graded. fits_instead rests on the Hughes 2013 sunscreen RCT. No safety rows: no interaction found in the sources opened.

items.name: Electrolyte drink mixes (LMNT, Liquid I.V. and similar)
items.evidenceFor: holding onto fluid and sodium better than plain water during long or very sweaty sessions
items.evidenceSummary: For long or very sweaty sessions, drinks with sodium help the body keep fluid, a use sports medicine groups support. For ordinary days, the research shows little beyond what water and meals already give, and no clear link to cramps.
items.humanQuestion: Is this for long, sweaty sessions or most days?
items.fitsInstead: Water on ordinary days, saving a stick or a pinch of salt for long, sweaty sessions.
items.notesInternal: Dose fields are mg of sodium per litre of drink during sessions over about an hour (ACSM 1996 stand, 0.5 to 0.7 g/L); one LMNT stick holds 1,000 mg, so dose is never the problem. 'trains' here really means sessions over an hour or heavy sweating: the 1996 stand found little difference from water under an hour. The 2007 ACSM stand's numeric sodium advice is paywalled and was not checked; only its abstract was read. Both hydration-index trials were beverage-industry funded (Maughan 2016 by the European Hydration Institute; Millard-Stafford 2021 by Coca-Cola), so the B rests mainly on the ACSM stands; resting trials disagree on electrolyte-only drinks, hence C otherwise. V3 was close (C overall, 'water does this') but its 'keto: keep' rule had no source I could find, so it is dropped. Cramps: no consistent link with hydration or electrolytes (Costa 2026), so 'cramps' is not a supported reason. Hyponatremia in ultras tracks overdrinking, not low sodium supplements (Hoffman 2015). LMNT's own page claims 4 to 6 g sodium a day is optimal, well above the 2,300 mg ceiling the NKF page gives. Wearable: no reliable signal on ordinary days. Safety rows supported by He 2013 (salt and blood pressure), LMNT label (1,000 mg sodium, 200 mg potassium per stick) and the NKF CKD sodium page.

safety.note: One stick adds about 1,000 mg of sodium, and more sodium tends to mean higher blood pressure, so a check with a clinician comes first.
Kidneys that filter less can let sodium, fluid and potassium build up, so the kidney care team gets the first say.

items.name: Pre-workout supplement (caffeinated multi-ingredient blend)
items.evidenceFor: a small lift in workout energy and performance, from the caffeine it carries
items.evidenceSummary: The caffeine in a scoop gives a small, well-studied lift in energy, strength and endurance. Many other ingredients come in small or undisclosed amounts. At a typical 250 mg, even a midafternoon scoop can trim that night's sleep.
items.humanQuestion: What time of day do you usually train?
items.fitsInstead: A large coffee about an hour before training covers the caffeine part for less.
items.notesInternal: Tier A rests on the caffeine (ISSN 2021 stand; Grgic 2020 umbrella review of 21 meta-analyses, moderate-quality evidence, mostly young men), not on the blend: I found no meta-analysis of multi-ingredient pre-workouts, product trials are small and often brand-linked, and 44% of listed ingredients sit in proprietary blends with beta-alanine below its effective dose (Jagim 2019). 89% of regular users take it for energy and focus (Jagim 2019 survey), which is why evidence_for names energy as well as performance. V3 graded B and said the sleep cost starts 'after 2pm'; Gardiner 2023 modelled a standard 217.5 mg pre-workout needing about 13.2 h before bed to avoid lost sleep (before 8:50am for a 10pm bedtime), so afternoon and evening scoops cost more than V3 implied. dose_min 140 mg = 2 mg/kg at 70 kg, the ISSN 'may be as low as' figure; 3 to 6 mg/kg (about 200 to 400 mg) is the consistently effective range, so a stim-free tub fails DOSE_BELOW_MIN. tier_otherwise N: no studies of pre-workouts outside training; for alertness alone, coffee carries the same caffeine. Coffee as a substitute is my inference from caffeine being the shared active ingredient, not a head-to-head trial. Safety rows: pregnancy and breastfeeding from EFSA and FDA plus Jagim 2019's 254 mg average serving; heart from Bella 2025, Jagim 2019 (self-reported heart abnormalities) and the energy-drink ECG trials; under-18 extends AAP 2011's energy-drink guidance to stimulant pre-workouts; medicines from FDA and Gardiner 2023 (antidepressants and oral contraceptives change caffeine half-life).

safety.note: FDA suggests talking with a provider about caffeine limits while breastfeeding, and a scoop is a large dose.
Stimulant blends have been linked to heart rhythm and blood pressure changes, so a check with a clinician comes first.
Some medicines make caffeine stronger or slower to clear, so a pharmacist can say whether a scoop fits.
One scoop often holds more than the 200 mg of caffeine a day judged safe in pregnancy, so a clinician check comes first.
Pediatric guidance keeps stimulant drinks out of teen diets, so Distill never suggests a pre-workout under 18.

items.name: Coffee after 2pm
items.evidenceFor: shorter, lighter sleep when caffeine is taken within about nine hours of bed
items.evidenceSummary: Across 24 studies, caffeine cost about 45 minutes of sleep and some deep sleep, more when taken later or in bigger doses. A regular cup's cut-off sits around nine hours before bed, and the loss is easy to miss.
items.humanQuestion: Is the afternoon cup about the caffeine or the break?
items.fitsInstead: A decaf, half-caf or black tea keeps the afternoon break with far less caffeine.
items.notesInternal: Tier A grades the sleep cost, so EVIDENCE_REGULAR is deliberately left out of keep_when: a strong tier on a cost item is not a reason to keep it. Same choice for energy drinks and evening alcohol. V3 was wrong on its headline number: in Drake 2013, 41 minutes was the self-reported (diary) loss at six hours, which did not reach significance (p = 0.08); the home EEG monitor measured more than an hour lost (1.1 to 1.2 h across the 0, 3 and 6 h conditions). Drake was funded by Zeo, the maker of the monitor, not a caffeine brand; n = 12. V3's '5 to 6 hour half-life' is narrower than Gardiner 2023's 2 to 10 h range across healthy adults. Gardiner's model puts a 107 mg cup's cut-off 8.8 h before bed (1:12pm for a 10pm bedtime), so '2pm' fits a bedtime around 11pm and is generous for earlier sleepers; black tea (47 mg) had no cut-off. Included studies were mostly low-to-moderate habitual users; tolerance in heavy users is unclear. dose_typical is caffeine per cup (Gardiner 107 mg per 250 mL; FDA 113 to 247 mg per 12 oz). cost_month_usd 40 is my estimate for a mix of cafe and home or office cups; moving the cup earlier saves nothing. Safety rows supported by EFSA and FDA (pregnancy, breastfeeding, medicines) and Gardiner 2023 (antidepressants, oral contraceptives).

safety.note: FDA suggests talking with a provider about caffeine limits while breastfeeding.
Some medicines, including certain antidepressants and birth control pills, slow caffeine clearance, so an afternoon cup can linger longer.
Pregnancy guidance keeps caffeine to about 200 mg a day in total, which one large coffee can reach.

items.name: Energy drinks (Red Bull, Monster, Celsius and similar)
items.evidenceFor: shorter, lighter sleep from the caffeine, growing the later in the day a can is drunk
items.evidenceSummary: The caffeine trims sleep just as coffee's does, and some cans hold three cups' worth. Students who drank energy drinks more often slept less and woke more. Blood pressure also rises for a few hours after a can.
items.humanQuestion: Roughly what time is the last can of the day?
items.fitsInstead: A smaller can before 2pm, or a cold sparkling water when it's mostly the fizz.
items.notesInternal: V3 was wrong that energy drinks have 'more effect on resting heart rate': the meta-analysis found no significant heart-rate change (+0.8 bpm, Shah 2016), and with caffeine matched at 320 mg an energy drink raised QTc and systolic pressure more than caffeine alone while heart rate did not differ (Fletcher 2017). V3 graded B; the sleep tier A comes from the caffeine meta-analysis (Gardiner 2023), since a can is a caffeine dose. Energy-drink-specific sleep evidence is cross-sectional (Kaldenbach 2024: 53,266 Norwegian students aged 18 to 35, a good age match), so it supports but does not carry the A. EVIDENCE_REGULAR left out because the tier grades a cost. dose_typical uses FDA's 54 to 328 mg per 16 oz range; the engine should read the actual can. Sugar, taurine and other ingredients were not graded here. Safety rows supported by AAP 2011 (under-18), Shah 2019 and Fletcher 2017 (QTc in healthy young adults), Shah 2016 (blood pressure), FDA and EFSA (pregnancy, breastfeeding, medicines).

safety.note: A single energy drink raised blood pressure by a few points for hours, so with high blood pressure a check comes first.
FDA suggests talking with a provider about caffeine limits while breastfeeding.
Large servings lengthened a heart rhythm measure (QTc) even in healthy young adults, so a heart condition means a clinician check first.
Some medicines make caffeine stronger or slower to clear, so a pharmacist can say whether a can fits.
Some cans hold over 300 mg of caffeine, past the 200 mg a day judged safe in pregnancy.
Pediatric guidance says stimulant energy drinks do not belong in children's or teens' diets.

items.name: Alcohol in the evening
items.evidenceFor: less REM sleep after evening drinks, already at two or fewer and growing with each one
items.evidenceSummary: Across 27 studies, up to about two drinks already trimmed REM sleep, and more drinks trimmed more. Overnight heart rate also climbs with each drink. Falling asleep faster showed up only around five drinks.
studiedForms: alcohol dosed by body weight in lab studies
items.humanQuestion: Mostly with friends, or more of a solo wind-down?
items.fitsInstead: Same plans, with the last drink a little earlier or the second one alcohol-free.
items.notesInternal: V3's 'HRV down 10 to 25 percent' misread Pietila 2018: the 9.3 and 24.0 figures are percentage-point drops in Firstbeat's HRV-derived 'recovery' score at low and moderate intake; RMSSD itself fell 2.0 and 5.7 ms, and heart rate in the first three hours of sleep rose 1.4 and 4.0 bpm (8.7 at high intake). That study is observational (within-person, 4,098 Finnish employees, mean age 45, effects stronger in younger people) and two authors worked for Firstbeat. V3's 'fall asleep faster' at one or two drinks is not supported by the meta-analysis: Gardiner 2025 saw faster sleep onset only at about five drinks, and total sleep, efficiency and night waking were too uncertain to call. The older qualitative review (Ebrahim 2013) reported faster onset and second-half disruption at all doses, so the two disagree on those points while agreeing on REM; the A applies to REM. V3's 'shows up the same night on every wearable' has no source. EVIDENCE_REGULAR left out because the tier grades a cost. dose_typical is grams of pure alcohol for one to two US standard drinks (14 g each). Frame as what a drink costs, never as stopping; social drinking is often LOVED and kept. Safety rows supported by the US container health warning (27 CFR 16.21), CDC breastfeeding guidance, NIAAA pages (medicine interactions, liver, mental health, legal age 21) and ADA 2026 recommendation 5.19 (delayed lows with insulin or secretagogues).

safety.note: CDC calls not drinking the safest choice while breastfeeding, with at least two hours per drink before nursing.
With insulin or similar medicines, alcohol can bring on low blood sugar hours later, so glucose checks after drinking matter.
Heavy drinking strains the liver, so any liver condition makes alcohol a question for a clinician first.
Alcohol can deepen low mood, anxiety and sleep trouble, and interacts with some psychiatric medicines. If cutting back feels hard, that's a conversation for a clinician.
Alcohol interacts with many common medicines, from sleep aids to pain relievers, so a pharmacist check comes first.
US labels carry the Surgeon General's advice against alcohol in pregnancy because of the risk of birth defects.
Distill leaves alcohol out entirely below the legal drinking age, which is 21 in the US.

items.name: Late dinner (within 2 to 3 hours of bed)
items.evidenceFor: more night waking when the main meal lands within about three hours of bed
items.evidenceSummary: Findings are mixed. Surveys tie eating within three hours of bed to more night waking and reflux, yet a 10pm-dinner lab trial found unchanged sleep stages. One small trial saw lower nighttime heart rate with earlier meals.
items.humanQuestion: Late by choice, or is that when work ends?
items.fitsInstead: On late nights, a lighter dinner, with more of the day's food at lunch.
items.notesInternal: V3 graded B and said eating late raises overnight heart rate and body temperature. I found no source for body temperature. For heart rate, the only trial I found runs the other way round and in an older group: finishing eating at least 3 h before sleep lowered nighttime heart rate and raised HRV as secondary outcomes in 39 adults aged 36 to 75 with overweight (Grimaldi 2026). For sleep, the one polysomnography RCT (Gu 2020, 10pm vs 6pm dinner, healthy adults around 26) found no change in sleep stages; surveys link eating close to bed with more night waking (Chung 2020, ages 18 to 29; Iao 2022, US time-use data); a one-week crossover in 16 adults aged 18 to 35 found lower melatonin and more breathing events with heavy late eating (Kesgin 2025); a heavy 10pm protein-and-fat meal disturbed self-rated sleep in young men (Ucar 2021). Disagreement plus small trials gives C. The reflux link (Fujiwara 2005) is a case-control association in reflux patients. dose_typical is the gap between finishing dinner and bed, in minutes. Several sleep-cost items (this, evening alcohol, late caffeine) share the same nights; worth testing one at a time so wearable effects don't blur. Safety row supported by ADA 2026 recommendation 5.28 (consistent carbohydrate timing with fixed insulin doses).

safety.note: With set insulin doses, meal timing is part of the plan, so moving dinner is worth planning with the care team.

items.name: Meal delivery or meal-prep service (meal kits or ready meals)
items.evidenceFor: eating a healthier diet, or losing weight, with ready-made or pre-portioned meals
items.evidenceSummary: Independent research is thin. In a small two-week trial, meal kits and ready meals both lifted self-rated diet quality. The weight-loss trials of prepared meals were mostly funded by the companies whose meals were tested.
items.humanQuestion: Does most of the box get eaten each week?
items.fitsInstead: A smaller plan with fewer meals a week, or a Sunday plan and batch cook.
items.notesInternal: V3 graded B ('works if the food gets eaten') with no source. The weight-loss RCTs of prepared meals I found were company-linked: Rock 2016 was funded by Nestle, maker of the entrees (confirmed in the paper's full text); Rock 2010 is reported in press coverage of its disclosure as funded by Jenny Craig, whose program it tested (not verified in the paper itself). Both were in adults with overweight and included counselling. By the brief's rule brand-funded studies count as none. Independent evidence: one pilot RCT (Hollis-Hansen 2023: 70 food-pantry clients, free meals for two weeks, self-rated outcomes, no no-meal control group) and a 2025 scoping review that found only nutrient-calculation studies of meal kits, no intervention studies. Graded C on the small, short pilot; honestly close to D for paying 22-to-35-year-olds. The real clear code is UNUSED (food that goes uneaten). how_common 3 from Boyar 2025 (18% of US adults used a meal kit in the past week, more among younger, higher-income, health-minded people). cost_month_usd 350 blends meal kits (about $300) and ready-meal plans (about $450); my estimate, not sourced. fits_instead batch-cook idea leans on Ducrot 2017 (meal planning tied to better diet quality, cross-sectional). No safety rows: none found.

items.name: Morning sunlight (10 minutes outdoors)
items.evidenceFor: a body clock that runs earlier, so sleepiness comes earlier at night
items.evidenceSummary: Bright morning light nudges the body clock earlier; in one camping study, a week of natural light moved it about two hours. A review links brighter mornings with earlier, better-rated sleep. Ten minutes hasn't been tested directly.
items.humanQuestion: Is it for sleep, or more for the morning itself?
items.notesInternal: V3 fact-check target confirmed: Wright 2013 (8 campers; clock about 2 h earlier after a week of natural light only; read in full text). Tier B is for clock timing only: lab bright-light experiments in healthy adults agree (Dautovich 2019 review, 32 experimental + 13 observational studies, no meta-analysis), but no trial tested 10 minutes outdoors, and everyday wrist-measured light shows weak or conflicting links (Bohmer 2021). Mood or energy claims would be tier C. V3 dayOne line ('about half of one night's normal swing') had no source and is dropped. clear_when empty: free, B tier, and the wake-up light rule keeps the free option. Area set to sleep (V3 batch was mind); reviewer may move it back. Never tell anyone to look at the sun.

safety.note: Some medicines, such as doxycycline or isotretinoin, make skin burn faster; sunscreen is fine, since the light that counts reaches the eyes.
With sun-sensitive skin, shade or sunscreen keeps morning light gentle, and a dermatologist can advise on limits.

items.name: Meditation app (Calm, Headspace)
items.evidenceFor: a small, short-term drop in stress and anxiety
items.evidenceSummary: Across dozens of trials, mostly in people without a diagnosis, mindfulness apps eased stress and anxiety a little over a few weeks. Gains were small, follow-ups short, and real-world use usually fades within a month.
items.humanQuestion: When did you last open it?
items.fitsInstead: A free guided meditation app, for the same kind of practice without the subscription.
items.notesInternal: V3 tier B kept. A is arguable (Linardon 2024: 45 RCTs, effects held in lower-bias trials), but effects are small (g 0.24 to 0.28), measured only at post-test (10 days to 8 weeks), not better than active therapies, and the authors flag possible conflicts of interest in Headspace trials (k = 15; Calm k = 5). Gal 2021 stress effect (g 0.46) was heterogeneous (I2 68%). V3 line about sleep ('people say they sleep better; measured change smaller') was not checked here and is removed. Baumel 2019 backs the UNUSED path (median 30-day retention about 3%, meditation apps about 5%). V3 cost 15 reflects monthly billing; annual plans run about $70 a year, so 7 is a blended estimate (prices from third-party pages, not sourced). Safety note from Farias 2020.

safety.note: Meditation now and then stirs up anxiety or low mood; if that happens, a therapist can help shape a gentler practice.

items.name: Journaling or a worry list before bed
items.evidenceFor: falling asleep a little faster
items.evidenceSummary: In one sleep-lab study of 57 young adults, five minutes writing a specific to-do list for the coming days led to falling asleep faster than listing finished tasks. Other small trials of worry writing are mixed.
studiedForms: specific to-do list for the coming days
items.humanQuestion: Is it a to-do list, or more of a feelings journal?
items.fitsInstead: Five minutes listing tomorrow's tasks in detail, the version tested in a sleep lab.
items.notesInternal: V3 tier B lowered to C: one single-night PSG study (Scullin 2018, n = 57, healthy 18 to 30, d = 0.63) plus small mixed trials (Harvey 2003 pilot: shorter self-reported latency; Mooney 2009 in insomnia: no latency change). V3's '9 minutes faster' appears in Baylor University's own write-up (opened), not in the paper's text, which reports the effect size and shows means in a figure I did not read; keep the number out of person-facing copy unless verified. The tested form is a specific to-do list; a feelings journal is a different practice with weaker sleep evidence. BORROWED_WEAK listed because it is C tier, but it is free; the engine may want cost to weigh in. Area set to sleep (V3 batch was mind).

items.name: Gratitude practice (journal, list or letter)
items.evidenceFor: a small lift in everyday mood and life satisfaction
items.evidenceSummary: Studies from 28 countries, nearly 25,000 people, find a small average rise in well-being, clearest for positive mood. Other pleasant exercises do about as well, and how often it's done mattered little.
items.humanQuestion: Does it still feel good, or more like homework lately?
items.fitsInstead: Once a week instead of nightly; in studies, how often mattered little.
items.notesInternal: V3 tier B raised to A: Choi 2025 (PNAS, preregistered, 145 papers, 24,804 people, g = 0.19, robust to publication bias). The effect is small and not specific to gratitude: Davis 2016 and Choi 2025 both find it matches other positive activities, and Davis found no effect on anxiety. Number of sessions did not moderate the effect (Choi), which supports the weekly fits_instead. Awe 'moral' is a judgment call: it fits when the practice dwells on other people's kindness (Keltner's moral beauty), much less for lists of pleasant things; blank it if the reviewer prefers. clear_when empty: free and A tier.

items.name: Breathwork (box breathing, 4-7-8, physiological sigh)
items.evidenceFor: feeling calmer and less stressed
items.evidenceSummary: Small trials agree that regular breathwork eases stress modestly. Over a month, five daily minutes of long-exhale sighing lifted positive mood more than mindfulness. In a lab test, six slow breaths a minute raised HRV more than box or 4-7-8.
studiedForms: slow breathing near 6 breaths a minute
items.humanQuestion: Is it for tense moments, or a daily habit?
items.notesInternal: V3 tier B confirmed. Fincham 2023: 12 RCTs, 785 adults, g = -0.35 for stress, moderate risk of bias, effect significant in nonclinical samples; first author trained as a breath teacher. Balban 2023 (n = 108, remote, WHOOP-measured; senior author advises WHOOP): breathwork beat mindfulness on positive affect only; anxiety and negative affect fell equally in both, so V3's 'beat mindfulness for mood' holds for positive mood only. HRV rises acutely with slow breathing (Laborde 2022, 223 studies), confirming V3; V3's 'less carries into the night' had no source and is dropped. 4-7-8 and box breathing have little direct evidence: in one session, 6 breaths a minute raised HRV more than either (Marchant 2025, n = 84). Hyperventilation-style breathwork (for example Wim Hof) is a different item with fainting risk and is not covered here. wearable_sees partial: heart data shifts during a session; overnight carry-over unproven.

items.name: Therapy or counselling
items.evidenceFor: easing depression and anxiety for people who seek help
items.evidenceSummary: Hundreds of trials find talk therapy, especially CBT, eases depression and anxiety symptoms, with gains still present 6 to 12 months later. It's clinician-led care, so Distill never suggests letting it go; changes belong with the therapist.
items.humanQuestion: Would you like it counted in your monthly total?
items.notesInternal: Protected: never_clear yes and clear_when empty by design; no fits_instead offered for clinician-led care. Evidence population is people with depression or anxiety disorders, not healthy adults; no evidence_requires code fits, so it is set to none and the population sits in evidence_for. Keep the V3 behaviour of letting the person hide it from the cost total (hence the human_question). Cost: about $143 to $174 a session self-pay versus about $23 in-network copay (third-party 2026 figures, not sourced); 300 a month is a blended estimate for weekly sessions (V3 said 400). The safety row is a protection rule rather than a sourced interaction.

safety.note: Any change to therapy is best talked through with the therapist first.

items.name: Work email after 9pm
items.evidenceFor: what late work email does to switching off and sleep quality
items.evidenceSummary: Studies following workers link more after-hours email with switching off less and lower measured sleep quality, not shorter sleep. These track patterns, not cause; in a small trial, a phone-free half hour before bed meant falling asleep sooner.
items.humanQuestion: Is it expected at work, or more of a habit?
items.fitsInstead: One set check in the evening, then notifications off until morning.
items.notesInternal: V3 tier C kept. V3 said late work goes with lower HRV; I found no support: Kubo 2021 found no link with morning cortisol, and Wendsche 2017 found detachment unrelated to physiological stress markers, so the HRV claim is dropped. Evidence is observational (Wendsche: 91 samples, mostly self-report; Kubo: n = 58 with actigraphy, sleep quality but not duration). He 2020 tests phone restriction in general, not work email. Cause may run both ways: poor detachment can drive late email. Could not open the abstracts of Lanaj 2014 (late-night smartphone use, OBHDP) or Kushlev 2015 (email batching, CHB), so neither is cited. also_serves 'sleep' here means the habit touches sleep, not that it helps it.

items.name: Checking the sleep score every morning
items.evidenceFor: how the morning number shapes mood, energy and sleep worry
items.evidenceSummary: Trackers mostly feel good to use. In small experiments, a fake low score left people with insomnia feeling less alert that day; in healthy sleepers, one low score didn't change sleep. Score worry tends to cluster with insomnia.
items.humanQuestion: Does the score change how the day feels?
items.fitsInstead: A weekly look at trends, with the daily score hidden.
items.notesInternal: V3 tier C kept, now sourced. Orthosomnia evidence: case series (Baron 2017), cross-sectional screening (Jahrami 2024: 3% to 14% of a 523-person sample depending on cut-off), survey (Lundekvam Berge 2026: negative effects higher with insomnia). Experiments: Gavriloff 2018 (insomnia, n = 63) fake low feedback left people less alert and more tired; Draganich 2014 (n = 164) assigned sleep quality predicted 2 of 4 cognitive tests; Robson 2022 (healthy, n = 54) one fake score changed neither arousal nor diary sleep. No trial compares daily checking with not checking. V3 said worry about the number makes sleep worse; the experiments show effects on next-day feelings, not on sleep itself, so that claim is softened. wearable_sees no: the effect is on how the day is judged, which device data cannot separate. Keep V3's offer to hide scores.

safety.note: With insomnia or anxiety, a daily score can add worry; hiding it for a while is worth raising with a clinician.

items.name: Second wearable (Oura plus WHOOP)
items.evidenceFor: learning more about sleep and recovery than one device shows
items.evidenceSummary: We found no study testing whether a second tracker adds insight. Worn together in a sleep lab, Oura, WHOOP and Apple Watch each tracked total sleep well and stages only roughly, so two mostly repeat each other.
items.humanQuestion: Which one do you actually like wearing?
items.fitsInstead: One device, whichever is more comfortable to wear day and night.
items.notesInternal: V3 tier N kept and now sourced: no study tests the added value of a second device. Miller 2022 (n = 53, one lab night, six devices worn at once; the lab receives WHOOP support, though WHOOP had no role in the study) found all valid for total sleep and weaker on stages, each with its own HRV bias, so two devices can disagree with no way to tell which is right; that can feed score worry (see the sleep-score row). V3's 'they measure the same things' is right for sleep timing and heart rate, less so for stages and HRV. Ryan 2019: wearables mostly feel positive; anxiety shows up when unable to wear one. Rosman 2024 (atrial fibrillation patients) supports the heart-condition safety row. Cost: WHOOP about $199 to $359 a year, or Oura $5.99 a month plus the ring (third-party pricing, not sourced); 20 a month set as the typical extra cost (V3 said 30).

safety.note: If a clinician asked for a device to watch heart rhythm, keep that one and check before changing anything.

items.name: Nicotine pouches or vape
items.evidenceFor: a faster heart rate after use, and lighter, more broken sleep when used near bedtime
items.evidenceSummary: Nicotine near bedtime makes sleep lighter and more broken, in lab trials and in people tracked at home. Vapes nudge heart rate up a little; strong pouches raise it sharply, a 6 mg pouch only slightly.
items.humanQuestion: Did it replace cigarettes, or start on its own?
items.fitsInstead: Daytime only, with the last one a few hours before bed.
items.notesInternal: V3 tier A lowered to B. Sleep: small placebo-controlled patch trials in healthy non-smokers agree (Jaehne 2014, n = 66; Choi 2017, n = 16; also opened Gillin 1994 and Davila 1994, not cited), backed by actigraphy cohort data (Spadola 2019: nicotine within 4 h of bed, lower efficiency, about 6 more minutes awake) and a cross-sectional meta-analysis of vape-only users (Gulati 2026, OR 1.38). No sleep trial used pouches or vapes directly. Heart rate: dose-dependent; the pouch study (n = 15 smokers) found 20 to 30 mg pouches raise it 12 to 25 bpm but 6 mg only slightly; vaping about +2 bpm in a meta-analysis of mostly non-randomized studies. V3's 'lowers HRV' is not confirmed (Choi 2017: no overnight HRV difference). Withdrawal can upset sleep for a while (Jaehne 2009), so an evening-off test may look worse at first. If the pouch or vape replaced cigarettes, Distill should not propose letting it go; no safety condition code fits this, so it is flagged here and asked in human_question. The engine still needs V3's timing question (daytime only, some after 6pm, mostly evening). EVIDENCE_REGULAR left out of keep_when because the tier grades harm, not benefit. kind 'food-drink' is the nearest allowed value (no substance kind). Keep V3's stance: test evening timing, never a quit programme. Cost: ZYN about $5.50 to $6.25 a can retail, several pouches a day, about $80 a month (third-party pricing, not sourced; V3 said 60).

safety.note: Nicotine nudges blood pressure up after each use; a clinician can help weigh what fits.
Nicotine passes into breast milk, so any plan for it is best made with a clinician.
Nicotine raises heart rate and blood pressure after each use, so changes are best planned with a clinician.
Nicotine reaches the baby during pregnancy, so any plan for it is best made with a clinician.
US law sets 21 as the minimum age for nicotine products, so Distill offers no timing or strength tips here.

items.name: Strength training
items.evidenceFor: strength and muscle
items.evidenceSummary: Lifting reliably builds strength and muscle in healthy adults, and two sessions a week is enough to see it. Large studies also link 30 to 60 minutes a week with a longer life.
items.humanQuestion: How many days a week does lifting usually happen?
items.fitsInstead: Two full-body sessions a week, enough to build strength and muscle in trials.
items.notesInternal: V3 tier A confirmed (Currier 2023 network meta-analysis, full text). V3 gave no dose: pooled trials show 2+ sessions a week with 2+ sets reliably build both strength and muscle; one multi-set session a week still built strength, but once-weekly single-set arms had credible intervals crossing zero. The longer-life link (Momma 2022) is cohort data with a J-shaped curve, best near 30 to 60 min a week. also_serves 'mind' rests on Noetel 2024, which studied people with clinical depression (very low certainty), so it stays internal and out of person-facing text. clear_when is empty on purpose: training itself is never proposed for letting go. Safety: Riebe 2015 abstract names the ACSM screening factors (current activity, known disease or symptoms, planned intensity); the clearance rule itself is the well-known ACSM algorithm, full text paywalled. Pregnancy note rests on WHO 2020 and the NHS page. wearable 'partial': sessions log, but strength gains barely show in heart data (Reimers 2018 found strength training's resting heart rate drop less consistent across sexes than endurance training's).

safety.note: With a known heart condition, a clinician check before starting or stepping up hard lifting is the standard advice.
Strength work is encouraged in pregnancy; tell the coach, and avoid lying flat on the back for long later on.

items.name: Zone 2 cardio (3+ hours a week)
items.evidenceFor: aerobic fitness and a lower resting heart rate
items.evidenceSummary: Steady cardio reliably raises fitness and lowers resting heart rate. Studies don't show zone 2 beats other intensities, and mixing in some harder efforts adds a little more fitness.
items.humanQuestion: Do the long easy sessions feel good, or like homework?
items.fitsInstead: Brisk walking, which counts as moderate cardio toward the same weekly minutes.
items.notesInternal: V3 tier A kept for the outcome actually studied: aerobic fitness and resting heart rate from steady endurance training (Milanovic 2015, healthy adults 18 to 45; Reimers 2018). Not graded: 'zone 2 specifically'. Storoschuk 2025 (abstract) finds no evidence that zone 2 is the best intensity and says the enthusiasm draws on elite endurance athletes. V3's HRV claim and its 'Sandercock 2005' pointer were not opened, so HRV is dropped from the claim. dose_typical is MINUTES PER WEEK (WHO 150 to 300), not per session; 3+ hours a week sits inside that range. clear_when is empty on purpose: the cardio is never proposed for letting go; the lighter version lives in fits_instead. also_serves 'mind' rests on Noetel 2024 (walking or jogging, clinical depression, low certainty), internal only. awe 'nature' assumes outdoor runs, rides or hikes.

safety.note: With a known heart condition, check with a clinician before starting or ramping up long cardio sessions.

items.name: 10,000 steps / daily walk
items.evidenceFor: fitness and blood pressure
items.evidenceSummary: Walking programs raise fitness and trim blood pressure in trials. Large studies link more daily steps to a longer life, with much of the gain by 7,000 to 8,000; 10,000 is a round goal, not a threshold.
items.humanQuestion: Do you walk with someone, or is it alone time?
items.fitsInstead: A steady 7,000 to 8,000 steps a day, where large studies see much of the benefit.
items.notesInternal: V3 tier A kept but re-pointed: V3 named sleep and mood with no source; the graded outcome is fitness and blood pressure from walking RCTs in inactive adults (Murtagh 2015; lipids did not change). Steps and a longer life is cohort evidence: Ding 2025 curves bend around 5,000 to 7,000; Paluch 2022 finds mortality levelling at 8,000 to 10,000 for adults under 60, the age group this app serves. So fits_instead says 'much of', not 'all of', the benefit. dose_unit is blank because the allowed units have no steps option; proposing 'steps/day' as a unit. V3's 'one day's walk changes that night's sleep a little' was not checked and is dropped. also_serves 'mind' rests on Noetel 2024 (clinical depression) and Ding 2025 (fewer depressive symptoms at 7,000 steps, cohort), internal only. clear_when empty on purpose.

items.name: Gym membership
items.evidenceFor: strength and fitness, from the visits that happen
items.evidenceSummary: Regular training builds strength and fitness, and a gym makes that easier. The benefit lives in the visits: in one large study, monthly members averaged about four visits a month, paying more per visit than a pass.
items.humanQuestion: How many times did you go in the last month?
items.fitsInstead: A pay-per-visit pass, which often costs less when visits are few.
items.notesInternal: V3 graded the membership itself A. Now the A belongs to the training it makes possible and holds only for people who use it (evidence_requires 'trains', tier_otherwise N). The main clear codes are UNUSED and OVERLAP. Usage evidence: DellaVigna and Malmendier 2006 (7,752 members of three US clubs; monthly members averaged about 4.3 visits, over $17 a visit, when a 10-visit pass cost $10 a visit). V3's visit thresholds (8+ a month keep; under 4 for two months running) are unsourced but line up with WHO's 2+ strength days a week, roughly 8 visits a month. cost_month_usd 50 is my estimate (budget gyms roughly $10 to $25, mid-tier $40 to $70), not sourced. wearable 'partial': workouts show up, the membership does not. Proposed 'gym floor access' group for two gyms doing the same job.

items.name: Premium gym membership (Equinox, Life Time)
items.evidenceFor: strength and fitness, from the visits that happen
items.evidenceSummary: Training works the same in any gym, and no study we found shows pricier clubs bring better results. The extra money buys comfort, classes and spa rooms, which pay off only when used.
items.humanQuestion: Which parts of the club do you actually use?
items.fitsInstead: A standard gym with the same racks and machines, often for a fraction of the price.
items.notesInternal: No study found that compares outcomes by gym price, so the tier is the training's, applied only when the club gets used (otherwise N). Main clear codes: UNUSED and OVERLAP. V3's 'twice a week or more is worth almost any price' is opinion and is removed; V3's '$83 a visit' day-one copy is fine as arithmetic but not evidence. Premium clubs usually include a sauna or steam room, so proposed 'spa amenities' (with bathhouse or recovery-studio memberships) and 'gym floor access' (with a standard gym) groups. cost_month_usd 250 is my estimate (Equinox roughly $200 to $300+, Life Time roughly $100 to $250+), not sourced.

items.name: Boutique class membership (Barry's, SoulCycle, F45, Orangetheory)
items.evidenceFor: aerobic fitness from regular interval-style classes
items.evidenceSummary: Interval-style classes raise fitness at least as well as steady cardio in trials. A class format alone gives only a small edge over training solo; groups that feel like a team do better.
items.humanQuestion: How many classes did you make it to last month?
items.fitsInstead: A smaller class pack for the one or two classes booked most.
items.notesInternal: V3 said 'class formats have better attendance than open gyms, which is the honest case for paying more'. Not supported by what I opened: Burke 2006 found standard exercise classes did no better than home programs with some contact, while cohesion-building 'true groups' did best; Kritz 2026 (71 studies) found small, non-significant group edges for activity and health, and a significant edge for physical function only after removing outliers. Tier A is for the interval training itself (Milanovic 2015, healthy adults 18 to 45); no independent studies of the branded formats were looked for or found. Main clear codes: UNUSED and OVERLAP. Unflagged safety signal: spinning-induced rhabdomyolysis in healthy first-timers (Kim 2015, 11 cases); no schema condition fits, so suggest an item-level note such as 'ease into a first spin class'. awe 'collective' is for synchronized group classes; the row itself is a service. dose_typical 2 to 3 follows WHO-style weekly training, not a figure from the opened abstracts. cost_month_usd 200 is my estimate, not sourced.

safety.note: With a known heart condition, check with a clinician before high-intensity classes.
Tell the instructor about the pregnancy, ease the intensity as needed, and stop if overheated.

items.name: Yoga or pilates studio
items.evidenceFor: lower stress and better mood
items.evidenceSummary: Trials find yoga and pilates ease stress and lift mood, and yoga lowers resting heart rate and cortisol. Most studies are small and short, but the results point the same way.
items.humanQuestion: Is the studio more about the workout or the calm?
items.fitsInstead: A smaller class pack plus free follow-along sessions at home.
items.notesInternal: V3 tier B kept, outcome narrowed to stress and mood. V3 also claimed sleep benefits; not checked, so dropped. Support: Pascoe 2017 (42 RCTs against active controls, physiological stress markers, mixed populations), Pascoe and Bauer 2015 (25 RCTs, authors call it preliminary), Fleming and Herring 2018 (8 small pilates trials, inactive controls). Noetel 2024 ranks yoga among the stronger exercise types for clinical depression (very low certainty), internal only. Main clear codes: UNUSED and OVERLAP. The hot-yoga caution in pregnancy is in ACOG 804's full text, which I could not open (paywalled); the safety note rests on the NHS page (keep cool, stop if too hot, avoid lying flat on the back later). dose_typical 1 to 3 is common trial practice, not pulled from an opened abstract. awe 'collective' is for synchronized group practice; the row itself is a service. cost_month_usd 180 is my estimate (reformer pilates usually costs more), not sourced.

safety.note: Tell the instructor about the pregnancy, pick unheated classes, and avoid lying flat on the back for long later on.

items.name: Personal trainer
items.evidenceFor: strength from regular coached sessions
items.evidenceSummary: Coached training builds strength like any solid program. Small studies find a modest extra strength gain with a coach, partly from lifting heavier loads. The value rests on sessions that actually happen.
items.humanQuestion: Would the workouts still happen without the trainer?
items.fitsInstead: A few sessions to learn a plan, then monthly check-ins.
items.notesInternal: V3 graded A with 'strong evidence that this works, if you'd otherwise skip'. The supervision-specific evidence is small: Fisher 2022 (exploratory, 12 studies; strength SMD 0.40 with a wide CI; trivial body-composition effect) and Mazzetti 2000 (about 20 trained men, 12 weeks). Tier A is the training's; the coach adds a modest, uncertain extra. Nothing I opened shows that a trainer improves attendance; that V3 premise is untested here. V3 had no overlap group and treated low use as cost-per-session only; now UNUSED (unused or expiring session packs) is the main clear code, plus a proposed 'coaching' overlap with paid coaching apps. never_clear 'no': a trainer is not clinician-led care (a physical therapist would be a different row). cost_month_usd 400 assumes roughly $60 to $100 a session, 1 to 2 a week; not sourced.

items.name: Cold plunge or ice bath
items.evidenceFor: less muscle soreness after hard exercise
items.evidenceSummary: Cold water after hard exercise eases soreness a little. The mood and dopamine claims rest on few, small studies, some using hour-long soaks. Plunging right after lifting can blunt muscle growth, so spacing the two apart makes sense.
items.humanQuestion: Is the plunge for sore muscles or for the mood?
items.fitsInstead: A 30 to 90 second cold finish to a shower, free and tested in a large trial.
items.notesInternal: V3 tier C changed: B for soreness in people who train (Machado 2016: small edge over passive rest, best near 10 to 15 C for 10 to 15 min; Moore 2022: soreness, perceived recovery and power better at 24 h after high-intensity work), C for everyone else (Cain 2025: 11 RCTs in healthy adults; stress lower only at 12 h; no mood change in the one mood study; sleep and quality of life each rest on a single study; inflammation up right after). Well supported: a small soreness benefit. Popular but thin: mood, dopamine, immunity, resilience. The dopamine figure that circulates traces to Sramek 2000, a one-hour head-out immersion at 14 C, not a 3-minute plunge. Buijze 2016: cold showers cut sick-leave days but not illness days. V3's 'an evening plunge can make it harder to fall asleep' is NOT supported: Robey 2013 and Chauvineau 2021 (small, trained men, lab sleep tests) found no change in sleep onset, and Chauvineau found fewer night arousals. V3's blunted-growth point is confirmed (Roberts 2015; Pinero 2024 applies to cold water within about 15 min after lifting). Popular 2 to 5 minute plunges are shorter than the 10 to 15 minutes best studied for soreness. Key mismatch: the overlap file lists 'cold-plunge-ice-bath-tub-owned', but the V3 row key is 'cold-plunge-ice-bath' and had no overlap group; see overlap_proposals. Safety: Shattock and Tipton 2012 for heart rhythm; the pregnancy, diabetes, blood pressure and medication rows rest on standard tub label warnings (read in a combined hot and cold tub manual, CSC Chill1000), which also flag alcohol and drowning risk. The schema has no alcohol or plunging-alone condition, so suggest an item-level caution: ease in, never alone, never after drinking. kind 'device' assumes an owned tub; a DIY ice bath would be 'practice'. cost_month_usd 100 is my estimate (tub amortized over a few years plus power), not sourced.

safety.note: Cold water pushes blood pressure up, so with high blood pressure a clinician check comes first.
Tub makers list diabetes among the conditions to clear with a clinician before cold immersion.
Cold shock spikes heart rate and can upset heart rhythm, so a clinician check comes first.
Some medicines change heart rate, blood pressure or alertness, so a quick clinician or pharmacist check is worthwhile.
Tub makers advise checking with a clinician before cold immersion during pregnancy.

items.name: Sauna (after a workout or in the evening)
items.evidenceFor: heart and blood vessel health over the long run
items.evidenceSummary: A Finnish study following men for about 20 years links frequent sauna use with fewer heart deaths, and one small trial found lower blood pressure. Sauna for sleep is barely tested, though warm baths before bed speed up falling asleep.
items.humanQuestion: Is the sauna mostly for unwinding, or for heart health?
items.fitsInstead: A hot bath or shower an hour or two before bed, for the wind-down.
items.notesInternal: V3 tier B changed to C. The longer-life and heart link is one observational cohort of 2,315 Finnish men aged 42 to 60 (Laukkanen 2015; 4 to 7 sessions a week had a sudden cardiac death HR of 0.37 versus once a week, while the 2 to 3 sessions CI crossed 1; sessions over 19 min also linked lower). Trials are few and small: Lee 2022 (47 inactive adults with risk factors, 8 weeks, systolic 8 mmHg lower than exercise alone) and Hussain and Cohen 2018 (40 studies, only 13 RCTs, mostly under 40 people). A search turned up no meta-analysis of RCTs showing a consistent blood pressure effect. Well supported: very little beyond short-term blood pressure dips; popular: longevity, recovery, sleep. V3's 'an evening sauna helps many people fall asleep faster' has no controlled sauna trial behind it that I could find; the warm-bath meta-analysis (Haghayegh 2019) backs the fits_instead instead. V3 safety 'not with alcohol' is confirmed (Hannuksela 2001), but the schema has no alcohol condition; suggest a cross-item note with 'alcohol-in-the-evening'. Hussain and Cohen report one small study (n=10) with a reversible drop in sperm production; no schema condition, internal only. cost_month_usd 0 because the gym or bathhouse rows carry the cost. dose_typical 2 to 7 spans the cohort's categories; the clearest links were at 4 to 7 sessions a week. Blood pressure and on-medication safety rows also lean on standard spa label warnings (high or low blood pressure, medication: consult a physician).

safety.note: Heat lowers blood pressure for a while, so with low blood pressure or blood pressure medicines, check with a clinician.
Unstable chest pain, a recent heart attack or a severely narrowed aortic valve call for a clinician's go-ahead first.
Some medicines change heart rate, blood pressure or heat tolerance, so a quick clinician or pharmacist check is worthwhile.
Saunas are considered safe in a healthy, uncomplicated pregnancy, though a clinician check first is wise.

items.name: Sunscreen (daily, broad-spectrum SPF 30+)
items.evidenceFor: slower visible skin aging with daily use
items.evidenceSummary: Daily sunscreen is one of the best-studied habits in skin care. In a 4.5-year trial of 903 adults, daily users showed no detectable rise in skin aging, and about a quarter less aging than occasional users.
items.doseTypical: SPF 30 or higher, at least 1 teaspoon for the face
items.humanQuestion: Do you wear it most mornings, or mostly on sunny days?
items.fitsInstead: A broad-spectrum SPF 30 moisturizer, so one bottle covers two morning steps.
items.notesInternal: Tier A rests on one large independent RCT (Hughes 2013: n=903, 4.5 years, government-funded) plus a systematic review (Ronsch & Bauer 2021) in which both photoaging trials favored sunscreen. That review calls the overall evidence base limited and notes guidelines put shade and clothing first, so a strict reading of 'several RCTs' could argue B. Both A and B keep it via EVIDENCE_REGULAR. The trial abstract gives no SPF; SPF 30+ and 1 teaspoon for the face are AAD advice. Skin-cancer outcomes are left out of person-facing text because they would be a medical claim. V3 overstated two things: 'nothing else on the shelf comes close' (retinoids have more photoaging RCTs) and 'the evidence is as strong as evidence gets'. kind=practice because the kind list has no topical-product option; propose adding one. UNUSED is included per its definition (a bottle can sit unused); drop it if sunscreen should never be proposed for letting go. No overlap group: if the table has an SPF moisturizer, SPF makeup or oral sun pills, propose a 'sun protection' group with keep-best-evidence. dose_unit is blank because the unit list has no % or teaspoon. how_common and cost are estimates.

safety.note: If a sunscreen stings, as can happen with rosacea, a mineral one with zinc oxide or titanium dioxide is often gentler.
A mole or spot that is new, changing, itching or bleeding is one to show a board-certified dermatologist.

items.name: Retinoid at night (retinol, or prescription tretinoin and similar)
items.evidenceFor: fewer fine lines and smoother skin after months of use
items.evidenceSummary: Retinoids are the best-studied ingredients for fine lines. Trial reviews show tretinoin and over-the-counter retinol both smooth fine lines over months, and in a 48-week trial a milder tretinoin worked as well with less irritation.
items.doseTypical: tretinoin 0.025 to 0.1%, or retinol around 0.4%, nightly or a few nights a week
items.humanQuestion: Is it prescribed, or one you picked up yourself?
items.fitsInstead: A drugstore retinol on two or three nights a week, at a fraction of a premium serum's price.
items.notesInternal: Tier A is for the class. Tretinoin has two systematic reviews (Sitohang 2022: 7 RCTs; Siddiqui 2024: 25 comparison studies), and both tretinoin and retinol were significant for fine wrinkles in a 23-RCT network meta-analysis (Lin 2025, which has internal inconsistencies and one co-author company affiliation). Over-the-counter retinol alone is closer to B (Kafi 2007: n=36, mean age 87, up to 3 times a week). The 2005 Cochrane photodamage review was withdrawn in 2015 over a sponsorship conflict, so it is not cited. Adapalene was not significant for fine wrinkles in Lin 2025 (very wide CI), so fits_instead points to drugstore retinol, not adapalene. never_clear=no because the row mixes OTC and prescription products; prescribed use is caught by the on-medication safety row, but splitting it into 'OTC retinol' and 'prescription retinoid' (never_clear yes) would be cleaner. V3 contradicted itself: goalNotes named overlap 'exfoliants' but overlapGroups was empty. A retinoid is not an exfoliant and should never be the step dropped, hence the proposed 'retinoid nights' group (keep-best-evidence). Pregnancy: the data show no clear harm but are underpowered (Kaplan 2015). The AAD says stop tazarotene, and most experts stop tretinoin and adapalene; the AAD does not address retinol, which is treated the same way as a precaution. The breastfeeding row rests on e-lactancia (APILAM, updated 2023-02-09, opened this session); LactMed was blocked by a captcha, so it is not cited. Concentrations need a % unit, which the list lacks. Lowest studied doses that worked: tretinoin 0.025% (Griffiths 1995), retinol 0.4% (Kafi 2007). Cost $25 (V3 had $40) is an estimate: drugstore retinol is about $10 a month, telehealth tretinoin $20 to 40, premium serums $30 to 45.

safety.note: Very little of a retinoid cream reaches the blood, and the usual advice while nursing is to keep it off the chest.
A prescribed retinoid stays as prescribed, and any change goes through the prescriber first.
Most experts advise stopping tretinoin and adapalene in pregnancy and avoiding tazarotene, so an obstetrician or dermatologist is the one to ask.
Retinoids are usually paused in pregnancy, so Distill does not suggest starting one.
Acne that has not settled after six to eight weeks, or skin with eczema or rosacea, is worth a dermatologist visit before adding a retinoid.

items.name: Vitamin C serum (topical, morning)
items.evidenceFor: a brighter, more even skin tone
items.evidenceSummary: Small, short trials suggest a vitamin C serum can smooth fine lines and lighten uneven tone a little over months, though it adds no extra hydration. Plain L-ascorbic acid at 10 to 20% has the most research.
items.humanQuestion: Is it more for dark spots, or the morning ritual?
items.fitsInstead: A budget serum with 10 to 20% L-ascorbic acid, the best-studied form.
items.notesInternal: Tier C (V3 had B). The only RCT-only review found 7 trials with 139 people in total (Correia 2023). A 2026 review of 44 studies says many were small, short, open-label or industry-sponsored. Reported effects: objective lightening and smoother skin; hydration was no better than placebo. V3 had stability backwards: L-ascorbic acid is the unstable form, while derivatives are stable but less studied, and in pig skin magnesium ascorbyl phosphate, ascorbyl palmitate and dehydroascorbic acid did not raise skin vitamin C (Pinnell 2001). FORM_NOT_ABSORBED therefore fits derivative-only or oxidized products. Derivatives do have small newer trials (Boghosian 2026), so present that code gently. V3's 'turned orange' check and 'opaque, airtight packaging' are common advice, but I found no independent source this session, so both stay out of person-facing text. Concentration needs a % unit: if one is added, set dose_min 10 (studied L-ascorbic acid serums ran 10 to 15%; Al-Niaimi 2017 says above 8% is needed and above 20% adds nothing) and add DOSE_BELOW_MIN. kind=practice because there is no topical-product kind; if the engine only applies FORM_NOT_ABSORBED to kind=supplement, this row needs an exception. Cost $30 (V3 had $60) is an estimate: budget serums are about $15 a month, premium ones $60 to 90.

safety.note: A dark spot that is new or changing is one for a dermatologist rather than a serum.

items.name: Retinol or retinoid plus an exfoliating acid on the same nights
items.evidenceFor: better results from using both on the same nights than on separate nights
items.evidenceSummary: No trial we found shows that a retinoid plus an exfoliating acid on the same night beats spacing the two out. Each can dry and irritate skin, and dermatologists note exfoliating alongside a retinoid can worsen dryness.
items.humanQuestion: Does your skin sting or peel on nights you use both?
items.fitsInstead: The retinoid and the acid on separate nights, or the retinoid alone.
items.notesInternal: Tier D for the practice. V3's B graded the warning, not the practice. No trial compares same-night layering with alternate nights, so the founder's 'adds irritation, not results' is reasonable guidance but not proven. Support: AAD says exfoliating alongside retinoids may worsen dryness and that starting several anti-aging products close together irritates; Lin 2025 links glycolic acid to more adverse events and finds it not significant for fine wrinkles (only for roughness); Griffiths 1995 shows a stronger tretinoin adds irritation without adding benefit. Counterpoint, brand data only: a J&J patent (US5646186, opened this session) claims 5 to 10% glycolic acid in the same formula cut irritation from low-dose retinol in 14-day patch tests, with no effect at 0.3% retinol. V3's 'alternating nights gives the same benefit' is also untested, so the summary avoids it. Cost $15 covers the extra acid only; the retinoid's cost sits in its own row. Cadence 'weekly' means several nights a week; the cadence list has no such option. how_common is an estimate.

safety.note: Retinoids are usually paused in pregnancy, and an obstetrician or dermatologist can say which acid, if any, fits.
With rosacea, the AAD advises skipping glycolic and lactic acids, so a dermatologist is the better guide for this pairing.

items.name: Two exfoliants (a scrub plus an acid, or two acids)
items.evidenceFor: smoother skin from a second exfoliant on top of the first
items.evidenceSummary: One exfoliant can smooth rough skin, and no study we found shows a second adds more. Over-exfoliating can leave skin red and irritated, glycolic and lactic acids raise sun sensitivity, and strong exfoliation can darken spots on darker skin.
items.humanQuestion: Which one leaves your skin feeling best the next day?
items.fitsInstead: One exfoliant that suits the skin, used less often the stronger it is.
items.notesInternal: Tier D (V3 had B with no source). No study compares one exfoliant with two; the evidence that one acid works comes from Lin 2025 (glycolic acid eased roughness in RCTs). The harms are guidance-backed: AAD on over-exfoliating, scrubbing flaring acne and darker skin; FDA on AHA sun sensitivity (fades within a week of stopping). V3 overstated with 'one of these is doing the job and the other is doing damage', and its blanket 'keep the acid, drop the scrub' goes too far: the AAD suggests a mild chemical exfoliant for dry, sensitive or acne-prone skin, but says oily, thicker skin can take stronger methods. The darker-skin pigmentation risk has no condition code; consider adding 'darker skin tone' as a note condition. The FDA page reports the industry panel's view that AHA products are safe at 10% or less and pH 3.5 or higher. Cost $15 (V3 had $25) is an estimate for the second product. Cadence 'weekly' means a few times a week.

safety.note: Salicylic acid is generally considered fine for a limited time in pregnancy, and the AAD suggests checking with an obstetrician or dermatologist first.
With rosacea, dermatologists advise stopping exfoliation altogether, and acne that keeps flaring is worth a dermatologist visit.

items.name: Multiple hydrating serums (two hyaluronic acid products)
items.evidenceFor: more hydration from a second hyaluronic acid serum
items.evidenceSummary: In a small trial, one hyaluronic acid cream raised skin hydration more than a plain cream. No study we found tests a second hyaluronic serum on top, and the second bottle is the same ingredient again.
items.humanQuestion: Do the two serums feel different, or about the same?
items.fitsInstead: One hydrating serum, or a moisturizer that already has hyaluronic acid or glycerin.
items.notesInternal: Tier N for the doubled practice: no study tests a second hyaluronic acid product, and there is no mechanism by which a second dose of the same humectant would add much. The evidence for a single HA product is itself thin and industry-linked. Pavicic 2011 had co-authors from Evonik and Novozymes (both ingredient makers). The Bravo 2022 review was L'Oreal-funded, so it is not cited. A single HA serum would sit around tier C. V3 graded this B with no source. Cost $20 (V3 had $50) is an estimate: budget HA serums cost $10 to 20 a month. The proposed keep-most-used rule gives the existing 'hydrating layers' group a tiebreak.

safety.note: Skin that stays dry, itchy or cracked despite moisturizer is worth a dermatologist visit, since conditions like eczema can look this way.

items.name: Magnesium (any form)
items.evidenceFor: falling asleep a little faster
items.evidenceSummary: Small trials in older adults with insomnia found people fell asleep about 17 minutes sooner, though the studies were low quality. A 2025 trial in adults who slept poorly found only a small change. Sprays and oils barely absorb.
items.humanQuestion: Which form do you take, and how many milligrams?
items.fitsInstead: A handful of pumpkin seeds or almonds at dinner, which adds magnesium for very little.
items.notesInternal: V3 graded B; regraded C. The only pooled data are 3 small trials in older adults with insomnia, moderate-to-high risk of bias, GRADE low to very low (Mah 2021). The one independent trial in younger adults (Schuster 2025, university-funded) found a small effect (d 0.2, p 0.049) with null secondary outcomes, and its capsules also carried about 1.5 g glycine. Arab 2023 calls the trial evidence inconsistent. V3's rule 'oxide = form not absorbed' is contradicted: two of the three pooled trials used magnesium oxide (500 and 729 mg elemental) and drove the positive result. Apply FORM_NOT_ABSORBED to sprays, oils and bath flakes only (Grober 2017). The threonate sleep trial is brand-funded (AIDP authors; Magtein supplied by Threotech) and 1 g of threonate gives only about 75 mg elemental, below dose_min. dose_min 250 mg elemental = lowest dose with a positive result (Schuster, bisglycinate before bed); Rawji 2024 notes the two negative trials used 100 to 250 mg. The 'low intake responds best' idea is exploratory only, so evidence_requires stays none. Cramps not graded here. NIH ODS magnesium fact sheet returned HTTP 403, so the kidney and medication safety rows rest on well-known label warnings. Cost is an estimate.

safety.note: Kidneys clear extra magnesium, so with kidney disease a clinician check comes first.
Magnesium can reduce absorption of some antibiotics and bone medicines, so doses are usually spaced a few hours apart.

items.name: Melatonin
items.evidenceFor: falling asleep a few minutes sooner
items.evidenceSummary: Pooled trials show it helps people fall asleep about 7 minutes sooner, and it eases jet lag well. Sleep doctors don't back it for ongoing insomnia, and more than 5 mg adds nothing measurable.
items.humanQuestion: Every night, or mostly for travel and schedule shifts?
items.fitsInstead: Keeping it for travel and schedule shifts, where the effect is largest.
items.notesInternal: V3's 7 and 8 minute figures confirmed (Ferracioli-Oda 2013: 19 RCTs, 1,683 people). V3's line 'more than 1 mg adds grogginess, not effect' is not supported: pooled effects rise with dose up to about 4 mg (Cruz-Sanabria 2024) and higher doses gave larger total-sleep gains (Ferracioli-Oda). The defensible 'less is more' line is that over 5 mg adds nothing measurable (Cochrane jet lag review; Cruz-Sanabria). AASM 2017 suggests clinicians not use melatonin for chronic insomnia (weak, very low quality, based on 2 mg prolonged-release in over-55s); the summary reflects this. Tier B because the effect is consistent but small and mostly measured in people with sleep disorders; the jet lag evidence in healthy travellers is stronger. dose_min 0.1 mg = lowest dose that improved sleep (Zhdanova 2001, insomniacs over 50; 0.3 mg restored normal night levels; normal sleepers unaffected); 0.5 mg works for jet lag. UNUSED left off because occasional travel use is a normal pattern. Cadence set to daily, though many people use it only some nights. Erland 2017 (supplement content survey) not opened; NCCIH page summarizes it. Cost is an estimate.

safety.note: Case reports describe clotting changes and bleeding when melatonin was combined with warfarin.
Safety research during breastfeeding is lacking, so a clinician's view comes first.
Blood thinners and epilepsy medicines call for medical supervision alongside melatonin.
Safety research in pregnancy is lacking, so a clinician's view comes first.
For anyone under 18, melatonin is a decision for a clinician and a parent.

items.name: Sleep gummies (blend)
items.evidenceFor: falling asleep a few minutes sooner
items.evidenceSummary: The melatonin inside is the only ingredient with consistent trial support, and it buys a few minutes. When 25 gummy brands were lab-tested, 22 were mislabeled, one had no melatonin, and one held about 3.5 times the label.
items.humanQuestion: How much melatonin does the label list per gummy?
items.fitsInstead: A low dose of plain melatonin, 0.5 to 3 mg, for about a third of the price.
items.notesInternal: V3 graded B; regraded C, which reflects indirect evidence. No independent trials of blended sleep gummies were found. The working ingredient is melatonin (tier B on its own), but gummy doses are unreliable (Cohen 2023: 22 of 25 mislabeled, 74% to 347% of label, one product with no melatonin but 31 mg CBD). Valerian, common in blends, got a weak recommendation against for insomnia from AASM 2017; the other herbs were not graded here. The router could lift this to melatonin's tier only when a melatonin dose is confirmed; a melatonin-free gummy should route with herb blends (C or D). The 'third of the price' line rests on my cost estimates (about 18 vs 5 USD a month), not a source.

safety.note: Melatonin lacks safety research during breastfeeding, so a clinician's view comes first.
The melatonin in most gummies calls for medical supervision with blood thinners or epilepsy medicines.
Melatonin lacks safety research in pregnancy, so a clinician's view comes first.
Gummies look like sweets, and lab tests found real doses up to about 3.5 times the label.

items.name: Ashwagandha (KSM-66 / Sensoril)
items.evidenceFor: sleeping a little better after 6 to 12 weeks
items.evidenceSummary: Five small trials, all run in India, found sleep improved modestly after 6 to 12 weeks, more so in people with insomnia. Stress scores eased too. Rare cases of liver injury have been reported.
items.humanQuestion: Do you take it more for stress or for sleep?
items.notesInternal: Area kept as sleep for this batch, but stress is at least as common a reason to buy it (also_serves mind). If a reviewer moves it to mind, the stress evidence grades similarly (Akhgarjand 2022: 12 RCTs, 1,002 adults, low certainty).
